extracted.intended_audience: high-school and undergraduate math olympiad students and instructors (problem solvers)
extracted.subtask_description: Problem-solving techniques, identities, and characterization theorems for geometry, trigonometry, and combinatorics problems typically encountered in math olympiads; includes both concrete necessary-and-sufficient conditions and heuristics for constructing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for cyclic quadrilaterals
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek cyclic quadrilaterals in geometry problems; identifying cyclic quads often yields equal-angle relations and useful perpendicularities/orthocenter conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly advises 'Look for the cyclic quads in the following problems.' Example consequences include equal inscribed angles (e.g., ∠AEN = ∠ABN), right-isosceles triangles, perpendicularity relations, and orthocenter identifications used to finish arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclic quadrilateral characterization (product-sum identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: AB·CD + AD·BC = AC·BD if and only if ABCD is cyclic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equality is given as a necessary-and-sufficient algebraic condition for a convex quadrilateral to be cyclic; can be used both to test cyclicity and to construct proofs by verifying the identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equiangular polygon — constant sum of distances to sides
rubrics_metrics.description: In a convex equiangular polygon the sum of distances from any interior or boundary point P to the polygon's sides is constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via area decomposition: express polygon area as sum of triangle areas from P to vertices or as sum (1/2) a·dk (a = side length). For regular polygons the fact is immediate; an arbitrary equiangular polygon can be 'expanded' to a regular polygon, altering the sum by a constant (sum of distances between parallel sides). Converse: for triangles constant-sum implies equilateral; not true for quadrilaterals (parallelograms share property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex roots-of-unity criterion for equiangular polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equiangular n-gon has side lengths a1,...,an (in counter-clockwise order) and ε = cos(2π/n) + i sin(2π/n) is a primitive nth root of unity, then a1 + a2 ε + a3 ε^2 + ... + an ε^{n-1} = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret side vectors as complex numbers; translate to common origin and sum equals zero. The converse is not generally true (gives conditions like parallelograms in n=4), but if positive ai satisfy the sum=0 then there exists an equiangular polygon with those side lengths. Use root-of-unity algebra for proving relations among side lengths (e.g., n=6 reductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilateral triangle complex-number characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A triangle with complex-number vertices a,b,c (or their complex coordinates) is equilateral (and oriented counter-clockwise) iff a + b ε + c ε^2 = 0 where ε is a non-real cube root of unity (ε = −1/2 + i√3/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses ε as the 120° rotation operator in the complex plane; algebraic manipulation shows rotation relations between sides. The relation is reversible: if the equality holds the triangle is equilateral with the specified orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Napoleon's theorem (centroids of equilateral constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If equilateral triangles are constructed externally on the sides of triangle ABC, then the centroids of those three equilateral triangles form an equilateral triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via complex numbers using the equilateral triangle condition a + b ε + c ε^2 = 0 and taking centroids (averages of vertices). The text gives a full complex-number derivation and mentions visual ('proof without words') interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torricelli (Fermat) point characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: For an acute triangle ABC, the point T minimizing TA + TB + TC (the Fermat/Torricelli point) is the unique interior point with ∠ATB = ∠BTC = ∠CTA = 120°; segments from vertices to centers of externally constructed equilateral triangles are concurrent at T, and the circumcircles of those equilateral triangles pass through T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof via 60° rotations: rotating around a vertex maps distances and yields collinearity/minimality criterion. Use this characterization as both a minimization and incidence property for constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carpets theorem (area-moving heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the floor of a region is covered by nonoverlapping carpets and we move one carpet, the area of overlap equals the uncovered area of the floor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple, shape-independent area argument is used to give elegant, computation-free solutions for area-equality problems. Apply by identifying two equal-area 'carpets' that would cover the room if nonoverlapping; the overlapping area equals the uncovered area, yielding equalities among subareas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pithot's theorem (incircle condition for quadrilaterals)
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex quadrilateral ABCD has an inscribed circle (is tangential) iff AB + CD = AD + BC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via tangent-length equalities: tangents from a common vertex to the incircle are equal, yielding AK = AN, BK = BL, etc., summing equalities gives the relation. Converse constructed by drawing circle tangent to three sides and showing it must be tangent to the fourth if the side-sum equality holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incircle existence equivalent to concurrence of angle bisectors
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex polygon (in particular a quadrilateral) has an inscribed circle iff its internal angle bisectors are concurrent (they meet at a point equidistant from all sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For quadrilaterals: if three angle bisectors meet at one point the fourth also passes through that point. Use concurrency as a practical check for the existence of an incircle.

rubrics_metrics.name: n×n standard array selection sum identity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the n×n array with entries a_{ij} = (i−1)n + j (consecutive blocks by rows), any selection of n numbers with all in distinct rows and distinct columns sums to n(n^2 + 1)/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: chosen indices in each row correspond to a permutation j1...jn; sum = ∑[(k−1)n + jk] = n ∑(k−1) + ∑ jk = n*(n(n−1)/2) + n(n+1)/2 = n(n^2+1)/2. Use permutation-sum argument when analyzing such arrays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-term array functional equation (xij + xjk + xki = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an n×n array satisfies x_{ij} + x_{jk} + x_{ki} = 0 for all i,j,k, then there exist numbers t1,...,tn such that x_{ij} = t_i − t_j for all i,j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive antisymmetry x_{ij} = −x_{ji}, set t_i = (1/n)∑_k x_{ik}, and verify x_{ij} = t_i − t_j. This is a standard linear-algebra/averaging reconstruction technique for such cyclic-sum relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue-difference pigeonhole strategy for modular table entries
rubrics_metrics.description: When table entries depend only on the difference i−j (mod n), selecting entries in distinct rows and columns forces the set of differences (i−j) to be a permutation of residues; summing these differences leads to modular contradictions used to show repetition among selected entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in the 10×10 example: if ten entries in distinct rows and columns were all different, the sum of differences modulo 10 contradicts the known sum of 0+1+...+9 modulo 10. Use residue sums and permutation properties for contradiction proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex-trig toolkit and de Moivre formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent z = cos θ + i sin θ; then zn = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ) (de Moivre). Useful formulas: cos θ = (z + z^{-1})/2, sin θ = (z − z^{-1})/(2i), cos nθ = (z^n + z^{−n})/2, sin nθ = (z^n − z^{−n})/(2i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities are presented and used repeatedly to derive trigonometric sums, products, and special-angle equalities (e.g., cos3θ = 4cos^3θ − 3cosθ). Use complex representation to reduce trig identities to algebraic manipulations of roots of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed forms for finite trig sums (Sn and Cn)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Sn = sin a + sin 2a + ... + sin na and Cn = cos a + cos 2a + ... + cos na, closed forms are Sn = (sin(na/2) sin((n+1)a/2))/sin(a/2) and Cn = (sin(na/2) cos((n+1)a/2))/sin(a/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by summing geometric series in complex form z + z^2 + ... + z^n and separating real/imaginary parts. These expressions are useful for evaluating finite trigonometric sums and solving related equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting twice (double counting) as a proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the elements of a set in two different ways (by rows vs columns, by grouping vs direct enumeration) to obtain identities or contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: committee-of-k-with-chair combinatorial identity (n choose k k = n * (n−1 choose k−1)), sequence-sum contradiction using sums of 7- and 11-consecutive terms arranged in tables, and many combinatorial equalities. Arrange the same multiset into different partitions/sums to compare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler totient divisor-sum identity via counting fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum_{d|n} φ(d) = n, where φ is Euler's totient function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial proof approach: consider the n fractions 1/n, 2/n, ..., n/n and group them by lowest denominator in reduced form; counts of numerators coprime to denominators yield the φ(d) contributions and sum to n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion as an incidence-transform technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inversion about a point (pole A) to transform circles through A into lines, converting circular-incidence problems into collinearity/line-incidence problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in the proof that a set S of points with certain modular-sum circle constraints must be concyclic: invert about A to map circles through A into lines and then use collinearity/minimal-distance arguments. Inversion simplifies many circle-intersection and concurrency problems.
